summary: The 19Al sample is the highest-Al member (Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu, at.%) of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel family studied in this paper (the "19Al" alloy), taken through the full processing route — vacuum induction melting, 1200 °C/24 h homogenization, hot rolling to 4 mm plate, and solution treatment at 1100 °C/10 min under argon with oil quenching — and then aged at 525 °C for 3 h followed by water quenching. It represents the shortest-time, lowest-temperature end of the aging window, in which the α (BCC) → β-Mn transformation is still very slow: the α matrix remains essentially untransformed and only a very small amount of β-Mn has formed, so hardness rises only moderately above the solution-treated baseline. The sample therefore anchors the low end of the alloy's flexible hardness range and illustrates how increasing Al content retards the precipitation kinetics of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%). EDS-measured chemistry of the 19Al alloy: Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6 and Cu 5.0 at.%. Compared with the sibling 15Al and 17Al alloys, the Al increase (15.0 → 18.6 at.%) is achieved essentially by substituting Al for Fe, while Mn (≈34.8–35.2 at.%) and Cu (≈5.0–5.2 at.%) stay nearly constant. Design intent: Al is the primary density-reducing element (≈0.1 g·cm⁻³ density reduction per 1 wt% Al) and is also expected to influence the precipitation and hardening behaviour of β-Mn; the high Mn level (35 at.%) is chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase; Cu is added to further promote β-Mn precipitation and raise hardness, based on the authors' prior Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloy work. The measured density of this alloy is 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes method), the lowest of the three alloys.
processing: Alloy ingots with the nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) were produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, then hot-rolled into plates 4 mm thick, which were cut by electrical discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for hardness measurement and microstructure characterization. The samples were solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere and oil quenched (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq). This sample — the 525 °C / 3 h condition — was then aged at 525 °C for 3 h and water quenched; it belongs to the aging series 525–650 °C / 1, 3, 6 and 10 h applied to the solution-treated state.
microstructure: After solution treatment the 19Al alloy is a single α (BCC) phase (EBSD phase map uniformly red; no γ/FCC resolved). The solution-treated 19Al grain structure is markedly finer and more equiaxed than those of the 15Al and 17Al alloys. At 525 °C/3 h the microstructure remains essentially a single α (BCC) matrix because the α→β-Mn transformation of the 19Al alloy is very slow at this temperature, so only a very small amount of β-Mn has formed. SE-SEM of this condition (50 μm scale) shows a uniform α matrix with no visible precipitate. Where β-Mn does form it is a Mn-rich phase that precipitates preferentially along α grain boundaries, with a minor amount of short rod-shaped β-Mn particles inside the α grains. The α→β-Mn transformation is thermally activated and slow in this highest-Al alloy: even after 10 h at 525 °C only about 12.1 % β-Mn forms, the lowest fraction among the three Al contents, and full transformation of the α matrix requires higher aging temperatures (a near-complete β-Mn matrix is seen only at 600 °C and above).
properties: Vickers microhardness (HVS-1000 digital tester, 9.8 N load, 15 s dwell, average of 5 measurements per sample): 574.1 ± 8.6 HV for this 525 °C / 3 h condition, versus the solution-treated baseline of 263.8 ± 1.1 HV for the 19Al alloy — a moderate increase that reflects the slow β-Mn precipitation at this low aging temperature. Because the β-Mn fraction formed at 525 °C is still small, this condition lies far below the alloy's peak hardness; the aging-hardening response of the 19Al alloy at 525 °C is gradual and fails to reach the peak (peak values for 19Al reach ~900 HV and the highest value, 917.8 HV, is obtained at 600 °C/10 h). Density of the alloy: 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes method). No tensile, fracture-toughness or nanoindentation data are reported for this specific condition (fracture toughness and nanoindentation were measured only on the peak-hardness samples). Characterization techniques applied to this alloy/condition: Vickers microhardness testing and secondary-electron (SE) SEM (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), on electrolytically polished samples; the broader alloy study also used XRD, EBSD and TEM.
mechanisms: Aging at the low temperature of 525 °C provides only a low atomic diffusion rate and a modest driving force for β-Mn formation, so nucleation and growth of β-Mn are extremely slow; after 3 h the α (BCC) matrix is still essentially untransformed and the hardness rise is only moderate (263.8 → 574.1 HV).

β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth must exclude large amounts of the other atoms to the surrounding matrix; the high Al content of the 19Al alloy (18.6 at.%) enriches Al around the growing β-Mn, which hinders its further precipitation and growth and slows the precipitation kinetics relative to the 15Al alloy.

Al strongly stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase in Fe-Mn-Al-based alloys; because β-Mn precipitation/growth requires the prior depletion of D0₃, the larger Al content (and the resulting increase in amount/size and stability of D0₃) further retards β-Mn nucleation and growth in the 19Al alloy.

Because β-Mn carries an ultra-high intrinsic hardness (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa measured by nanoindentation in the hardest 19Al sample, the highest among the three alloys), the degree of hardening tracks the volume fraction of β-Mn; at 525 °C/3 h that fraction is still very small, which is why hardness remains only ≈574 HV instead of the >900 HV reached when α is fully transformed.

β-Mn precipitates preferentially along α grain boundaries, with a minor amount of short rod-shaped particles inside α grains, consistent with faster atomic diffusion along grain boundaries than through the grain interiors.

Raising the aging temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation and growth through a higher driving force for β-Mn formation and an increased atomic diffusion rate; consequently the optimal aging window for achieving ultra-high hardness shifts to higher temperatures (575–625 °C) as Al content increases from 15Al to 19Al.
conclusions: This 525 °C / 3 h condition on the highest-Al (19Al) alloy captures the slow-kinetics end of the family's aging behaviour: the α→β-Mn transformation has barely started, the α (BCC) matrix is essentially featureless in SE-SEM at 50 μm, and hardness has risen only from the solution-treated 263.8 ± 1.1 HV to 574.1 ± 8.6 HV, far below the alloy's peak. Together with the sibling 15Al and 17Al data it demonstrates the paper's central finding that increasing Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn (full α→β-Mn transformation requires 6 h at 550 °C for 17Al and 10 h at 550 °C for 19Al, and only ~12.1 % β-Mn forms in 19Al after 10 h at 525 °C). Also, increasing Al slightly raises the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn by solid-solution strengthening yet lowers the overall hardening effect and fracture toughness because it decreases the amount of ductile FCC Cu-rich phase between the β-Mn interfaces. Practically, these Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels can be formed in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness level, enabling "one material, multiple uses" for lightweight structural applications.
